subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD RELIEF AND GRANT TO RED CROSS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD RELIEF AND GRANT TO RED CROSS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce that Canada is sending-indeed, the movement has already begun-approximately $2.5 million worth of food relief to the Middle East. Of this $1 million worth of wheat flour will be sent for distribution to Palestine refugees through the United Nations relief and works agency. The remainder will go through the world food program to the Arab countries of Syria, Jordan, Lebanon and the Yemen to meet food shortages there.
As an immediate emergency measure the government has also matched an initial grant of $20,000 from the Canadian Red Cross Society to the international committee of the Red Cross for medical supplies to help meet urgent needs arising from the recent conflict.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD RELIEF AND GRANT TO RED CROSS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the Prime Minister has said will meet with general support. However, in addition to the sums to which he has referred and assistance by way of food supplies and the like, there is one paramount question which I should like the right hon. gentleman to consider, namely the terrible possibility that thousands of Arab troops in the Sinai desert apparently face an awful death because of lack of water.
I hope action will be taken with some urgency in this regard. The United Nations has been meeting in a rather desultory way. Nothing has been done by the United Nations to meet this problem, one which cannot be postponed. This is a matter of life and death; and whatever may be the views of people as a whole toward the Arab position if ever there was a case demanding action it is the frightful situation which has developed in Sinai. I hope Canada will give a lead. Apparently the nations of the United Nations are devoting themselves to other matters, but unless we take action immediately to provide some hope of survival for those, whatever their numbers may be, wandering aimlessly over the desert, a sorry situation will be created. This will lead in years to come to resentment which will fester with the passage of time.
We have aircraft in the Middle East. Cannot they be used to convey assistance? Cannot something be done to rouse the United Nations to action now? Delay can only result in disaster and that frustration which comes to hopeless men.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD RELIEF AND GRANT TO RED CROSS
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, may I just say that this matter was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Calgary North and I had intended to deal with it on
orders of the day.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FOOD RELIEF AND GRANT TO RED CROSS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the people of Canada will support the expenditure which the Prime Minister has suggested for aid to refugees in the Middle East. The $2J million the Prime Minister has mentioned is a relatively small amount but it is a beginning, and I am sure, if on further investigation the government finds that more food and larger sums of money are required to help the refugees of this unhappy war, it will have the full support of the members of the house and of the country generally.
I would also like to associate myself with the plea which has just been made by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition with respect to the plight of the Arab refugees in the Sinai desert. Canada demonstrated when we were taking the Canadian forces in UNEF out of that area that we are capable of putting on a very efficient and effective airlift. I think the Canadian government might do well to

June 16, 1967
External Aid for Middle East offer the services of our air force and whatever helicopters can be moved to that area to take these people out of the Sinai desert just as quickly as possible. I know such a program, if the government were to undertake it, would have the wholehearted support of the Canadian people.
Whatever one may think about the reasons for the outbreak of hostilities, all of us want to see that human beings are protected against an agonizing death, also having in mind that any humanitarian actions we can take at this time will help allay some of the present bitterness and, we hope, might lay a foundation for better understanding in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all realize that there has been increasing concern right across this country with respect to the plight of those who are facing starvation and death in the Middle East. We in this group would like to associate ourselves with the expressions of commendation on the fact that the government has seen fit to take immediate action to provide the sum of $2J million to assist in meeting this problem.

However, I would like to ask whether there has been a concerted plan on the part of European and North American countries to join in this particular program. I think the program should be shared in by all, and not by just a few who perhaps are more than willing to step in and meet their responsibilities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of the termination of pregnancy has been the object of extensive study in the last few years, and also of legislation in several countries. Recently a bill has been introduced in the United Kingdom to amend and clarify the law relating to termination of pregnancy by registered medical practitioners. The present bill is inspired by its British counterpart and is for the purpose of allowing medical termination of pregnancy in certain cases under the surveillance of medical and governmental authorities.

Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet I should like to reply to the question raised yesterday by the hon. member for Calgary North and again today regarding the disastrous situation in respect of certain Egyptians in the Sinai desert. When this matter was first brought to our attention we got in touch with the Israeli government. After all, the Israeli army is in occupation of this territory and these particular people we are concerned with are members of the armed forces of the United Arab Republic.
We asked the Israeli government for information concerning what is being done and indicated our desire to help in any appropriate way to meet this and related problems on other parts of the border. This morning I have received information that the Israeli authorities are taking all possible steps to avert human suffering. To this end, during the past few days they have been sending air search units to locate the distressed persons in the Sinai. They were parachuting water and food to them wherever possible, and aiding their movement westward toward the Suez canal.
One of the difficulties in connection with helping these people has been that the water pipe lines under the Suez canal had been cut off. It is open again by action taken by the

U.A.R. government and the international Red Cross, but for a time there was no fresh water getting across the Suez canal by these pipes.

Mr. Chairman, in undertaking my new responsibilities as Registrar General I want to say to the house at the outset that I am vitally aware of the importance of the task given me, and since this is the first opportunity I have had to speak in this capacity I want to thank all hon. members who have sent me letters or who gave me words of encouragement. I undertake to do my best in this new job.
Last year the former president of the Privy Council explained the rationale of the department in the reorganization bill which set it up. At this stage I should like to say that I had the opportunity of being acting minister in this department for some time during the time of Mr. Favreau's illness. In all my dealings with him, not only serving under him but as a member of this house, I found him to be a Christian gentleman, always a conscientious member of the house and a conscientious minister. I am sure every hon. member here shares my regret that he was constrained to seek relief from the heavy responsibilities which he had here as a minister and as a member of parliament, and wishes him, as I do, health and happiness on the bench of the superior court of the province of Quebec.
This department is designed to bring together several agencies which have a role in defining, shaping and directing public policy in the economic field. On the one hand we have the task of ensuring that our market system is competitive, alive and vital and that public interest is protected in matters re'ating to combines, mergers, monopolies, restricted trade practices, bankruptcies, patents, copyrights, trademarks, corporations and the securities field.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
On the other hand we are just beginning to formulate the kind of role th->t within its constitutional jurisdiction the federal government can play in aiding and assisting the consumer to gain the maximum benefit and enjoyment under our economic system. There have been a number of federal agencies working in this field already Mr. Chairman, and our purpose will be to strengthen and co-ordinate their activities and to add whatever new programs are necessary to give the consumer full and equitable participation in-the market. In this fashion we link together the federal government's concern to see that both the supply and the demand sides of the market are healthy and in balance.
June 16. 1967

So, Mr. Chairman, I see a considerable role for this department. I feel it can help this country in responding to the many significant changes taking place in our economic life, and can contribute to the essential tasks of defining and refining the important relationships among business, the consumer, the investor and the government.
I think I should draw to the attention of hon. member the fact that certain key responsibilities of the department, or the subject matters lying within its jurisdiction, were referred last year, on July 22, to the Economic Council of Canada. The Economic Council was charged with studying certain important aspects of the responsibilities of the Registrar General. I think it would be useful if I read the terms of reference:
In the light of the government's long term economic objectives, to study and advice regarding:
(a)	the interests of the consumer particularly as they relate to the functions of the Department of the Registrar General:
(b)	combines, mergers, monopolies and restraint of trade:
(c)	patents, trade marks, copyrights and registered industrial designs.
That means, Mr. Chairman, that the consumer interest, the area of combines and mergers and the area of patents and copyrights have been referred for depth study by the Economic Council of Canada. It means that this department in bringing forth its policy must have due regard to the reference made to the Economic Council of Canada, and hopefully await the report of the Economic Council on several of these areas.
In the consumer field, in relation to a consumer division in the new department I am hopeful that the Economic Council will report very shortly. I would think the next priority would be in the combines area and then finally in the area of patents, trademarks and copyrights.
This is the first time that a department which was originally concerned with the legal aspects of government and government regulation has been linked to a vehicle of economic policy. So that we are combining for the first time, I would think, Mr. Chairman, the economic and legal tools for the furtherance of a department of economic policy.
Needless to say, in the department a considerable structure will have to be reoriented and built. In the consumer area, for instance, there are several agencies and various departments spread over the government service. In the Department of the Registrar General there has to be co-ordination, and personnel
Supply-Registrar General have to be recruited. The same feature, of course, applies in establishing a federal presence in the regulation of securities. We will also need to strengthen the bankruptcy forces, the combines forces and the corporate law forces of the department if we are to discharge the responsibilities which I am sure parliament and the Canadian people will rightfully impose upon us.
So one of my principal functions in the early stages, Mr. Chairman, is to analyse the structure from the basis of the best budgeting and program analysis possible in relation to the cost and benefits of the program that we hope to inaugurate and implement; and we will from time to time be seeking both internal and outside advice on these subjects.
I think it is important at the outset for members to recognize that the jurisdiction over many of the areas for which the Department of the Registrar General has authority is a shared jurisdiction with the provinces. This is particularly so in the corporate and securities field as well as in the consumer field. So that anything parliament and the government are able to achieve in these areas must be done in close co-operation with the provinces, and I undertake to achieve as best I can both full consultation and close co-operation with the ten provinces of this country.
I should now like to review some of the principal areas falling within my responsibility and for which I am rendering an account to this house. The first matter relates to bankruptcy. Members who have compared this year's fiscal estimates to last year's will notice that the increase in the estimates is due largely to an increase in staff from 27 to 72 positions in the bankruptcies branch as well as an increase from 81 to 102 positions in the combines branch. A close scrutiny of the estimates will reveal that virtually the entire increase in cost will be found to be the result of the increase in personnel and expertise in those two areas. Those increases, of course, reflect public interest and demand as they impose themselves upon the responsibilities that I have been given.

Bankruptcies have aroused much interest recently on account especially of the publicity that was given to some serious and most reprehensible abuses of the bankruptcy process which were uncovered in recent years. It must be agreed that these abuses are most serious and extremely reprehensible.
It is most important that we continue our policy of improvement in this field in order
1602	COMMONS
Supply-Registrar General that the confidence of our fellow Canadians in our system of free enterprise be not jeopardized. Furthermore, it is essential that the institution of bankruptcy itself be completely rehabilitated from the state of disrepute in which it has fallen in recent years, so that it may fulfil adequately the essential role for which it is designed in our modern society.
We intend not only to continue our policy, but accelerate the process of implementation of the measures which are necessary to achieve these goals.
The bankruptcy regional offices in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, the setting up of which had been announced at the time of the enactment of the amendments to the Bankruptcy Act in July 1966 have now been in operation for more than two months. The opening of these offices which are staffed with expert auditors and investigators, I am convinced, will be quickly recognized as one of the most progressive measures taken in a long time in the field of bankruptcies and will constitute our most effective weapon against abuses which have been uncovered in that field in recent years.
Although these offices have been in operation for a relatively short period of time, they already have, in many respects, proven their usefulness. With these regional offices in operation, we are in a position to intensify the much needed enforcement of the Bankruptcy Act with regard to offences of an administrative character. These offences, as announced by Hon. Lucien Cardin during the debate on motion for second reading of Bill No. S-17 to amend the Bankruptcy Act, are now prosecuted whenever necessary by the federal Department of Justice. We feel that it is most important that these offences be prosecuted vigorously if we want to stimulate in this field a sense of honesty and integrity which, in the past, has too often been lacking, not only on the part of some trustees but also on the part of some debtors and creditors alike. It is essential, by reason of the far-reaching effects of bankruptcy on debtors, creditors and society as a whole, that the integrity of the procedure be respected. We are prepared to take every step that may be necessary, not only to protect that institution, but also to ensure that it has the respect of all.
Hear, hear.

Hon. members are aware, of course, that the federal government occupies only a portion of the larger field of criminal law enforcement when we are dealing with bankruptcies. In the last few years, we have

DEBATES	June 16, 1967
intensified our ties with the provincial authorities. Each level of government is now very much aware of the nature and extent of its responsibility and the improved lines of communication and co-operation that have been, and are still in the process of being developed will bring about, I hope, a much better enforcement of the law in this field. Let us hope that this aggressive approach will serve as a good deterrent on those individuals who are too prone to use the bankruptcy legislation for their own selfish and illegal purposes.
Before leaving this subject, however, I should like to emphasize that the role of bankruptcy regional offices is essential in this field. Its expert auditors and investigators have already proved their usefulness and particularly have had the opportunity to help certain provincial and municipal authorities which are often faced with most complex and difficult problems.
[DOT] (12 noon)
With respect to our bankruptcy legislation itself, I might mention that there are many indications that the amendments of July 1966 to the Bankruptcy Act have already contributed a great deal to correct the abuses that they were designed to remedy. I am not thinking only of the increased powers of investigation of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy but other provisions as well, such as those concerning reviewable transactions, proposals, etc. It must be appreciated, however, that the enforcement of the Bankruptcy Act and the amendments of 1966, however effective and useful they might be, are not, by any means, the complete answer to all of the problems that we are facing in the field of bankruptcy nowadays.
So many developments have taken place in the field of consumer credit, financing, debt collection, commerce and business since 1949 that our present legislation needs to be completely re-appraised and re-assessed in the light of present day conditions. Our approach to bankruptcy problems must be rejuvenated and new solutions must be devised.
As an example of this, I might mention the problem of the wage-earners' or consumers' bankruptcies which, with the ever-increasing rate of consumer credit, is becoming more and more pressing. We have to ask ourselves whether the solutions that have been devised, many decades ago, for the businessmen and the traders are adequate in the case of consumers and wage-earners of present days. We
June 16, 1967

also have to ask ourselves whether our present legislation keeps a proper balance between the opposite interests of debtors and creditors in our changing business and commercial world.
The 1966 amendments dealt with this problem of the wage-earners' or consumers' bankruptcies by providing for an orderly payment of debt. Those provisions have been in force in Alberta since April 17 of this year and, in Manitoba, since June 1. I am not sure, on the other hand, that it might not be possible to find yet a better solution than that contained in the 1966 amendments to the problems of bankruptcies by wage-earners or consumers.
At all events, the report of the three men committee set up to assist the department in its revision of our bankruptcy and insolvency legislation will be, I am sure, most valuable in our study of those problems. We have not asked the committee to study and recommend measures aimed only at mere patching up our legislation. Nor have we asked the committee only to clear up the ambiguities, to recommend a new arrangement of the provisions of the act or to include some partial solutions liable to remedy the most pressing problems, as was done in 1949 at the time of the last revision of our Bankruptcy Act. On the other hand, we asked the committee to make a thorough examination of the legislation, to consider the very assumptions and the underlying principles on which it is based, in the light of present day conditions and practices. We also asked the committee to review all the various machineries and procedures provided by our legislation and to report on any changes it considers necessary concerning our legislation and its administration. This applies not only to the Bankruptcy Act but also to the federal Winding-up Act, the Companies' Creditors Arrangements Act and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangements Act.
I am following very closely the work of the committee and I am in a position to say that it has been most active since its very inception in February 1966. It has already drafted a good portion of the new Bankruptcy Act which the committee will eventually recommend to the government.
However, it must be recognized that effective bankruptcy legislation and a healthy and vigorous administration is not a cure-all solution to the various and complex problems that insolvency may bring about in our modern society. These various measures of which I have just spoken, Mr. Chairman, must be coupled with other legislation that can afford

Supply-Registrar General a degree of protection that is outside the scope of an ordinary bankruptcy legislation.
The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act would fall into this category, as would all these other measures that are primarily designed for the protection of the investors.

To summarize the present state of the policy on bankruptcy, important amendments to the Bankruptcy Act were enacted on July 11, 1966. The work of the advisory committee on bankruptcy also is progressing satisfactorily, though a draft bill completely revising the federal legislation in the field of insolvency and bankruptcy will not be ready for some time-probably not before early in 1968.
We have set up regional offices of the bankruptcy branch. They have been set up, since March, 1967, in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver and are staffed by bankruptcy investigators and accountants. The role of these offices is to implement the work of the bankruptcy branch with a systematic audit program of trustees, and to investigate alleged cases of irregularities connected with bankruptcies, whether those have taken place before or after the bankruptcy.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is cooperating closely with the bankruptcy branch and the regional offices in cases where fraud and other offences of a criminal nature are involved. This summer, between July 9 and 22, we have organized seminars for bankruptcy branch officers at Carleton Place.
We have continued our careful review of trustees' operations, and the licences of more than 60 trustees have either not been renewed or have been restricted to the administration of the estates in their hands.
The bankruptcy branch has circulated bulletins to assist trustees in upgrading their performance. No new trustees have been appointed since April, 1965. An interim policy for the licensing of trustees will be adopted very shortly.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I should like to pass now to the corporations field where we are studying a general overhaul of the Canada Corporations Act. The purpose of the amendments we wish to incorporate in the act is to bring the federal act into line with the new Ontario legislation as it relates to insider trading, proxy solicitation and so on-amendments which were effected in Ontario in 1966-and the general disclosure of information for the protection of shareholders, particularly minority shareholders.
1604	COMMONS
Supply-Registrar General
The Canada Corporations Act is now more than 30 years old. Intensive study will be necessary to ensure that this act may continue to play a useful role in the development of a modern, outward-looking and efficient Canadian economy. Changes in legislation are therefore seen in the act. Though amended extensively in 1965 and slightly in 1967, it is due for a complete revision because of the growing importance of corporate law and recent developments in connection with disclosure of information in the securities field.
I wish to announce to the committee the establishment of a task force to study the provisions and working of the Canada Corporations Act. The director of the force is Dr. Robert W. V. Dickerson of Vancouver and the associate director is Mr. Robert J. Bertrand of Montreal. The task force will have the services of a number of people who have worked on recent studies for the federal and provincial governments such as the Carter royal commission on taxation and the Kimber and Lawrence committees in Ontario. I am causing a press release to be issued at this moment and hon. members will receive a copy which will contain biographies of all the fulltime and part-time members of the task force. The members have now been assembled and have already held two full two day meetings. The work has been assigned and I have asked the gentlemen involved to follow a critical path approach and to submit their report to me on the specific problems put to them by September 15.
Speaking about task forces in general terms I believe a great deal can be said in favour of bringing in authoritative people from the academic world to give advice and assistance in any field to be reviewed and 1 am delighted with the calibre of the men who have agreed to devote their summer to examining the problems I have described. I believe in mobilizing where possible all the brains in the country for the solution of specific problems, since by using this technique we can bring fresh ideas into government and marshal the views of various interested groups by means of what I call a filter process.
After the task force has reported I hope to submit its conclusions to a reviewing panel of practising lawyers, accountants and representatives of the various interests involved. Then, of course, the departmental officials of the government will consider the results, putting them through another filter, as it were, and finally, when the bill is put to the House of Commons, I expect it will be referred to an

DEBATES	June 16, 1967
appropriate standing committee where hon. members and members of the public may have ample opportunity to scrutinize it and suggest improvements. Our object is to enlarge the scope of the Canada Corporations Act to make investment in Canadian corporations as attractive as possible to Canadian investors and to ensure the most effective investment of resources in Canada.
I pass now to the securities field. A study of the subject within the government is now in its preliminary stages. We are continuing the work wh ch was undertaken last summer to analyse the role the federal government ought to play in this field. When I spoke during the federal-provincial conference on securities matters last April, I envisaged that the federal initiative would lie in four areas. First, the federal government should encourage the provinces to adopt uniform legislation across the country and do everything it could to bring about uniformity. Second, we should establish a central repository of information on security matters, and this we have undertaken to do. Third, the R.C.M.P. would establish a fraud investigation squad, and their services in this field would be available to all provincial securities commissions. Fourth, we should contemplate the establishment of a federal presence inasmuch as the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction over international and interprovincial trading. I want to say that a federal presence in some form is necessary in the national interest. Of course, the cooperation of the provinces is essential and should be sought.
I may say there were two federal-provincial meetings, one in April and one which ended only yesterday. Some very interesting discussions were held and I hope we can envisage uniformity and the virtual elimination of duplication of administration for the better regulation of the capital market in Canada so as to encourage Canadians to invest with confidence in the securities of this country.
Perhaps I may pass now to the field of patents, copyrights and trade marks. My department is also responsible for the administration of legislation dealing with intellectual property. As hon. members probably know, this field was the subject in the late fifties of an extensive study by a royal commission under the chairmanship of the late Mr. Justice Ilsley. The reports by the commission on patents, copyright and industrial designs were tabled in the house in the early sixties but action on them is still forthcoming. My
June 16. 1967

officials were about to recommend legislation in line with the commission's recommendations when further progress was withheld following the announcement last July by my predecessor that the government had requested the Economic Council of Canada to undertake a study of certain important aspects of the responsibilities of the Registrar General and his department, including patents, copyright and industrial designs. I have already drawn this to the attention of the committee.
In the area of copyright also, legislative changes are unduly behind schedule. A number of representations have been received from time to time on behalf of interested organizations urging the government to act upon some of the Ilsley commission's recommendations. The present act requires almost complete revision and here again my officials are prepared to proceed with the drafting of new legislation as soon as the Economic Council reports.

Upon receipt of the final report of the special committee of the House of Commons on drug costs and prices, I immediately referred its recommendations to departmental officials and these have since been under intensive study. I want to take this opportunity, in my capacity as the minister responsible for the implementation of some of these recommendations, to congratulate the committee for the coherence of its report and for the research and fundamental review that the committee gave this very complicated and delicate subject.
The committee made a number of recommendations constituting a package program designed to bring about a lowering of the cost of drugs to the consumer. Some of these recommendations were directed to the government, some to the medical profession, and some to the industry, both the drug industry and the pharmaceutical industry.
My colleague, the Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget on June 1, announced the removal of the sales tax on drugs and other budgetary measures as part of a major government attack on high drug prices. These measures can only be a part of an effective program to reduce drug prices. The effect by itself of the removal of the sales tax and the lowering of the tariff, while beneficial and necessary to the general program of helping the consumer, will necessarily be limited. Indeed, according to the press some members of the industry have already indicated a somewhat extraordinary reaction to this action by initiating an immediate price increase.
Of the recommendations of the special committee directed to government, some would require legislation. These proposals will be considered on an urgent basis over the summer months and it is my intention that any necessary legislative measures will be announced to parliament in the autumn.
I have the responsibility, Mr. Chairman, of receiving the reports of the director of investigation and research of the combines branch. Turning now to developments relating to the Combines Investigation Act, as hon. members are aware and as I have already mentioned, the government requested the Economic Council of Canada to undertake a study of

Supply-Registrar General certain important aspects of the responsibilities relating to combines falling within the authority of the Registrar General of Canada.
When the estimates of the branch were before the house last year there was a discussion of the necessity for increase in staff. I said at the outset that the increase in our spending within this department over the last year related primarily to increase in staff within the combines branch and within the bankruptcy branch. With my full support a continuous program of recruiting professional staff has been in progress during the 1966-67 fiscal year, and the establishment in this respect was increased from 34 to 42 positions as of April 1, 1967. The actual strength on March 31, 1967, was 30 professionals, and since that time additions have been made and several offers of employment have also been made.
The director still considers that substantial staff increases are necessary to cope with the increased work of the branch but he is faced with the difficulty of recruiting, assimilating and training new staff, which necessarily places limits on the possibility of rapid growth of the branch. However, while the major part of the work of the branch must be carried out by officers on the permanent staff, the director from time to time has engaged special assistants for particular purposes and in appropriate cases is prepared to make use of outside assistants.
In increasing the staff of the branch particular attention has been paid to the question of staff for the research section. At the end of the fiscal year 1965-66, one officer had joint charge of the merger and monopoly section and research section, staff for research being drawn from the merger and monopoly section. The permanent professional staff of the section now numbers five, including an officer in charge and four economists, all these officials having joined the branch since April, 1966. In addition, two university professors and four graduate students have been retained by the section for the summer.
We are looking for new legal and economic talent, honed in commercial skills, to give more effectiveness to the branch.
The following research projects are presently under way: First, an inquiry into mergers in Canada in the post-war period 1945-1965, a very important and large scale analysis of all known mergers in the period, designed to assist the government in formulating any future policy in regard to mergers. Second, the branch is undertaking a study of service industries at present not


within the scope of the act, including professional sport. Third, the branch is undertaking a study of concentration in Canadian manufacturing industries.
I want to say that the department has an opinion from the Department of Justice that services are not currently within the ambit of the Combines Investigation Act but I would think, without trespassing on the reference to the Economic Council of Canada, that services constitute a considerable part of the gross national product and we should be thinking seriously about amending the act to embrace the service factor. I would also hope we could contemplate a stronger use of the trade and commerce clause, so as to give the act civil as well as criminal jurisdiction, and with a civil jurisdiction a power to insist on cease and desist orders.
We must also continue the scrutiny of the Combines Investigation Act as it applies to our exporting impetus because there is obviously a difference in the application of the act, recognized already by the statute, as it affects the domestic and export parts of our industry.
A matter of importance in the enforcement of the act has been the size of the fines imposed. While it has not been the general policy of the crown to ask for specific fines but rather to draw all relevant facts, including the seriousness of the offence, to the attention of the court, the policy now is that after obtaining and considering the recommendation of crown counsel in this respect he is instructed to request a minimum fine where the court invites a specific representation.
Until recently the largest single fine imposed was $25,000. In a recent case, however, individual fines ranging up to $150,000 were asked for by the crown. Although the maximum fine imposed on any individual company in this case was $75,000, the total fines amounting to $391,500, the crown is seeking leave to appeal against the amount of the fines levied.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I would like to address the committee on the matter of consumer interest. As all members of the committee know, there was reference in the speech from the throne to the establishment of a department, or a reorganization of the present department, into a department of corporate and consumer affairs. The legislation concerning the minister's authority and the departmental name-wTe are not yet wedded to any particular name-will be introduced at the present session of parliament in the fall. The
June 16, 1967	COMMONS
contents of the bill will be made known in due course in the proper way, and at that time I would hope we could have a full debate on the scope of the department.
I want to pay tribute to the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on consumer credit prices. I think that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and Senator Croll played an outstanding role, as did all members of the committee, in bringing the high cost of living and its relative aspects to the attention of the Canadian people and the House of Commons. I also want to applaud in particular members of the opposition who served on that committee, especially the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, who played a very crucial part in its decisions.
Further, I want to pay tribute to the efforts of the Consumers Association of Canada and other groups who contributed to the work of the committee. This committee is in the vanguard of a revolution in the committee system. This committee broke new ground. The use of the committee system in this fashion allows wide public debate. I believe it allows members to be better informed and through them allows the public to be better informed.
I think it strengthens the independence and widens the knowledge and participation of members and the people in the development of public policy. It calls upon the experts and the technocrats, both within and without the government service, to account for and explain the basis behind the policy judgments and decisions. It, of course, allows the private sector and business to bring their views directly into the legislative process. I think this is a very encouraging trend indeed. I should like to see the committee reconstituted in the fall so it may continue its work.

The broad objectives of the consumer program which the government intends to develop are the following: First, to give the consumer a voice in government; second, by legislation, research and education to improve the quality of consumer demand and to place the consumer in a better position to protect his or her own interest and establish his or her own choice more effectively. I said before that no department of government will be able to protect the consumer. All we can do is put the consumer in a better position to protect himself or herself by assuring that the market forces are fair and equal and that there is as much research, information and public education as possible made available so 27053-1031

Supply-Registrar General that the choices the consumer has to make in an increasingly complex economy are made clear to her. Third, we hope to provide for the orderly channelling of consumer submissions and inquiries which are made to government. Fourth, in consultation with the provinces we hope to work toward unification throughout Canada of a program of consumer protection. Here again it will be necessary to have the closest co-operation with the provincial agencies and departments which now, happily, are beginning to assume some responsibility for this area.
I should like to digress briefly to reply to some very interesting remarks made during the debate in reply to the speech from the throne by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. She took exception to the department having responsibility for both corporate and consumer affairs. She felt that consumers would be sacrificed to corporations. I hope I have stated her argument fairly and I hope she will contribute to this debate later this afternoon. I should like to say to her as respectfully as 1 can that I disagree. I should like to offer the suggestion to her that I feel she may be misconstruing the mechanics of the department. In order to put the consumer in a stronger position, two aspects of the market relationship must be scrutinized, that is, the supply aspect and the demand aspect, the seller or distributor on the one hand and the purchaser or buyer on the other.
On the supply side the whole field of competition must be looked into. There is the area of fair market practices; there is the area of disclosure so that there is sufficient information available for the investor or consumer. It relates also, on the supply side, to the methods which would enhance the validity of the consumer's choice. There is the matter of the method of packaging, labelling and weights and measures. All these aspects of the supply side involve corporations. They involve, on the part of companies and businesses in this country, self-discipline and selfregulation so that there are competitive forces at play and so that marketing practices are fair and not deceptive.
I would hope that by the concentration of this effort within a department of government we would be able to persuade industry and the mercantile interests to fulfil the objectives we have in mind. If we are unable to persuade them within our constitutional authority as a federal government, we have the power to regulate. This would involve the combines branch, the corporations branch, the securities branch and the bankruptcy branch.

Supply-Registrar General
On the demand side there is the necessity that the consumer be informed. This is the primary objective. It involves such things as education and research. The summary of my argument, therefore, is that in order to give the consumer proper representation and in order to give the consumer what protection we can within the limits of government we must have authority over both the demand and supply sides of the market relationship. Otherwise it would be ineffective.
It is not possible for me to state in greater detail at present the government's plans, because in accordance with what I have previously said we want to have the views and recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada when formulating the consumer program. As I said before, we hope these will be available shortly or at least before the fall.
In order to be effective the federal program must be developed carefully, deliberately and not hastily. I should like to suggest a number of reasons for this being so. The federal jurisdiction is limited in this field. We cannot, for instance, contempate direct controls such as price controls or the regulation of industry within this scope because ordinarily these are provincial matters. The federal government does not have jurisdiction over prices. Prices depend on competitive forces. We hope to ensure that the forces are truly competitive. Prices in general depend on the general economic and fiscal policies of the country. Second, we need to consult and liaise with the provinces. We need to do this in order better to supplement and integrate the existing and future provincial consumer programs. In the third place we must proceed carefully because it will take time to recruit and co-ordinate adequate staff. Finally, I believe it is a useful thing to know what we are doing before we do it, because I am very anxious that what we do shall become effective. It is all very well to go off in all directions like a chicken with its head off, but I feel this would only cause unnecessary distortions in marketing practices and would provoke more difficulties than it would solve. If I were to suggest something which perhaps is unCanadian, I might say I think we should have facts before we have policy. I intend to proceed with all deliberate speed in that fashion.
Within the consumers' interest, the department of the Registrar General will have responsibility for the relationship of business with the public, the investor and the consumer. We do not intend needlessly to interfere with the relationship between business and


the investor and consumer. We do not intend to tell the manufacturer what to produce. We do not intend to tell the retailer what to sell or at what price he should sell it. We do not intend to tell the worker where to work and we do not intend to tell the consumer what to buy. We believe in a free market economy. I feel that we should release the competitive forces. This means we must attack monopolies and prosecute seriously all price fixing. It means there must be fair selling practices. We need to do the best we can to ensure that there are fair selling practices. We believe in persuasion before regulation, but we believe in regulation if that becomes necessary. We intend to do that.
Finally, of course, there must be education of the public. The consumer must be equipped by all reasonable means to make valid choices and judge true prices. We hope we can make this a department for the average Canadian. I should like to say that we will place particular emphasis on ensuring that the lower income consumers, those under the poverty level, those who are on the fringe of poverty, those with disabilities and pensioners can expect to have the maximum purchasing power for every dollar.
In conclusion I should like to thank the committee for its courtesy in putting up with such a long statement. I felt that I should outline to the committee the general responsibilities of this department. I should like to say to hon. members through you, Mr. Chairman, that this is a new department. It is a department with an important effort, a pioneer effort. The interests of the consumer, the investor and the businessman are not the responsibility of the government alone but are the responsibility of all of us in all sectors of the economy. I want to say that all members of parliament have a direct responsibility. I welcome comments not only from the floor of the house but if at any time a member from any quarter in the house has any particular point of view to discuss we can meet on a formal or informal basis and discuss it. I welcome constructive criticism from all quarters in the house.

We seek in this department to become a voice for the consumer in the councils of government, but we also want to ensure that the business interests of the community are able to operate effectively and efficiently. The keynote of our approach is partnership between all the constituents-consumers, investors, business and government.
June 16. 1967

I should like to point out to the members of the committee that this is not an expansion of big government but a reorganization of the existing responsibilities of government. I was looking at the estimates before I came in here and comparing the revenues of this department against the expenditures. This department will cost the Canadian taxpayer, net, $1,278,500. This is a considerable sum of money. However, when that sum is considered in proportion to the $9.5 billion in the estimates we are not going to be one of the big spenders in government. I do not expect any appreciable increase in expenditures, and every increase will be directed primarily toward recruiting skilled personnel to help us achieve the objectives which I have tried to outline. I say this is a reorientation; it is a co-ordination of existing agencies.
I believe that the expenditures of government must be controlled and that priority in spending must be determined. It is on this basis that an effort such as this, being a new one within the federal government and an important one, needs the support, assistance and co-operation of all members in this house and of everyone interested in the problems with which we will be dealing. I say again that we welcome any suggestions and criticisms. We will seek the co-operation of everyone. I want to thank the committee.

I have listened with a great deal of interest, Mr. Chairman, to the minister who is a new minister with a new department. I believe he has given it a new look. I feel that the reorganization of some of these departments, particularly those related to this field, is a good thing because it means that some of these activities are being dusted off. As the minister said, some of them have been neglected for a long time. I am going to deal with the department in its various phases. The minister has responsibility for the general administration. He has responsibility for the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission which administers the Combines Investigation Act. He has responsibility for bankruptcy. He has responsibility for the corporations branch. He has responsibility for the patent and copyright branch as well as trade marks and a few other items which are thrown in.
I believe we have heard today a young man of the new generation. I have never been concerned too much about chronological age. I am more concerned about mental age and the ability of a person to keep abreast of the times. I think I can pay the minister this compliment. He is one of those men who
Supply-Registrar General belong to the new generation. Not only is he young chronologically but he is young mentally and is very aggressive and progressive. Mind you, I am going to make some reservations because even when we flatter each other we have to make reservations.
I would say to hon. members through you, Mr. Chairman, that we have been listening to a good advocate. After all, a counsel is a man who sells ideas just as a salesman sells products. I would say the minister is a great salesman. He ended up on the theme of great freedom without control. I am going to put forward particular criticisms of the department itself and what has gone on in the department, but not of the minister or the other members of the department. As I have said, they have dusted off a few of the things that needed to be dusted off. I will come back to that theme.
I still believe, in spite of what the minister has said, that this government-whether the minister has any responsibility for it I do not know-is bringing about more control of business than any government since confederation. I believe there is not much difference between Liberals and Conservatives when it comes to how we say things. However, I believe that the Liberals believe in control and regulation. This is the reason the minister ended on the theme he did because he is concerned that the public should know where he stands.
When I travel throughout this nation I find that businessmen, small and large, farmers and trade union people are concerned about government control and government regulation. Some of the great things the minister has recommended can be done without any element of control. We have today the biggest bureaucracy the country has ever seen. The figures for last year indicate that $1.57 billion was spent on bureaucracy in this country. When I use the word "bureaucracy" I am using it in the broadest sense. I do not intend any particular criticism of any of the members of our public service. I am one of those, and I have said it before, who believe we have probably the best civil service anywhere in the world.
I want to deal with a few of the important items raised by the minister, particularly the Combines Investigation Act. This act is certainly essential. I agree with the minister that just as we have to have a Criminal Code to set a moral standard for the people, so we have to have an act to set an economic moral
June 16, 1967

Supply-Registrar General Standard for business. There is always a danger-I know the minister is aware of it because of his experience as a lawyer prior to becoming a minister-in any group having power such as the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission has. The way the commission implements the law, the degree of harshness with which it is enforced, may prevent a company discussing matters which would enable it to be more efficient in competing with other companies at home or abroad. It was for this reason that when we amended the Combines Act at the time we were the government the then minister of justice, the hon. member for Kamloops, dealt with that very aspect. Certain exceptions were made for the fish industry so we could compete with Japan and other nations.
In so far as the Combines Investigation Act is concerned, the idea is to prevent any phase of business from getting a virtual monopoly. The interpretation of the act with regard to the word "virtual" is that degree of monopoly which is against the processes of law. It is unfortunate that in the past some of the great cases under the Combines Investigation Act, such as the sugar case and the brewery case, were dismissed because the evidence produced was not sufficient. In my opinion there was certainly a virtual monopoly in those cases from the layman's viewpoint, if not legally. As I say, those charges were dismissed, but that does not mean there were not competent lawyers prosecuting those companies.
In dealing with the Combines Investigation Act the minister talked about mergers. There are some mergers that may be very good and there are some which may create what I have referred to as a virtual monopoly. There is a new and, I think, dangerous trend today. I am as much against monopolies as I am against socialism. The kind of free enterprise which I think we should seek is one which would keep average-sized corporations in business. We oppose mergers of the kind where great monopolies in one field merge to control a whole industry, as in the case of the sugar industry in this country. When we have evidence of that the Combines Investigation Act should be used.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I want to mention something that I believe the Combines Act should look into, and I hope the minister will take note of this. The most expensive thing in Canada today, outside of paying income tax is dying. I have feceived letters about this matter. I am told
[Mr. Woolliams.J
that a monopoly exists today in the case of all the hardware that goes into making coffins. Some hon. members may feel this is a humorous topic, and perhaps it is. But because of this monopoly prices are set throughout the nation. I want to make sure that I do not leave the wrong impression in this regard. The fault is not that of the undertaker or the small funeral parlour in our cities, towns and villages. They have to pay a certain price for materials and that price if fixed. If you go anywhere in Canada you will find there is a virtual monopoly in respect of funeral prices today, not because of the undertakers but because of the monopoly in respect of hardware and the making of coffins.
The Combines Investigation Act should be enforced in this field. It may be found that those who control this monopoly-I will not name them here because I do not believe in carrying on an investigation in the House of Commons, and this information can be arrived at very easily-will be the cause of some sensitivity on the part of the government and other industries. An investigation may put the finger on the pulse of sensitivity in this respect. This virtual monopoly should be immediately investigated.
How much the Combines Investigation Act should be changed to fit new circumstances is something that can only be determined by the future progress of business in this country. I do not believe that the provisions of the act should be implemented too harshly. I am against the kind of decision that has been made in this regard. It seems, however, that the courts have followed this line. Where they found as a fact that there had been a virtual monopoly, say in the field of electrical supplies or plumbing equipment, even if the companies got together at a meeting in order to safeguard their businesses from insolvency and bankruptcy they were charged under the act. I was involved in one of those cases. The argument put forward by crown counsel at that time was that even if it was shown that the companies lost money they were still guilty under the act.
The act does not provide, of course, that there has to be a profit involved, but surely where companies in an industry because of new circumstances, perhaps automation or a change in the economic situation of the country, meet to solve some of their difficulties the act should not be too harsh with them. The act must be changed to fit new circumstances. Sometimes companies in an industry have to meet, and meet legally, in order to compete

for the domestic market and export trade. As I have said, if there were not some sort of combine in the fishing industry or other industries of this nation, we could not compete with the United States and Japan. We could not compete in this field if there were not some meeting and agreement among those in the industry. So much for the Combines Investigation Act, Mr. Chairman.
I now turn to the question of patents. This is an area where a young minister with young ideas can step in. Our patents are not recognized internationally; they are not worth anything outside Canada. I will use an example in this respect. A fellow named Goett in Calgary invented a new plow. It not only plowed the ground but pulverized it. You could go into a field cleared of brush and with this plow pulverize the roots and stumps to dust. This made the ground more fertile because the tree material was mixed with the soil. This was a new idea. This man came to my firm and asked us to obtain a patent for him. I have talked to many lawyers about this situation, and I am sure the minister is aware of it. After discussing the question with specialists in the city of Toronto I found that the only safeguard for this man, because big companies in the United States like Minneapolis-Moline and others wanted to get hold of the plow, was to patent the machine in Great Britain and then re-register it in the United States and Canada. This had to be done because the United States does not recognize a Canadian patent; they do not care about it. Words are only words and we can be too nice about these things.
This is only one of the many experiences I have had in the field of patents, and it is one field that needs to be dusted off and looked at very carefully. I hope the minister will give careful consideration to this question. To make patents effective we have to go to the authorities of the United States and Great Britain. It is a blow to our nationalism and our growth when a Canadian patent is good only in this country and is no good in Great Britain, the United States or anvwhere in the commonwealth. I know the minister has to be a little more careful than those of us who sit on this side of the house, but I am sure he will agree with me that Canadian patents are not worth anything outside this country. We are a nation of 20 million people but a Canadian patent does not mean much. In our trade with the commonwealth, the United States and other countries, patents are everything. Our patent law needs a complete overhaul.

I now come to a matter that is perhaps slightly outside the jurisdiction of the minister, but, after all, he sits with the Minister of Agriculture. I own some registered horses. In fact, I have in Alberta a stallion that was imported from Wales by the Duke of Windsor. This stallion and the horses are registered as purebreds in Great Britain. I can register them immediately in the United States without any trouble. The colts from that strain of Welsh ponies are registred in Canada. The certificates in this country are much prettier; you get a great big star and a lovely signature. I sent the certificate to Washington and they sent them back and said they did not recognized purebred stock registered in Canada. I have letters to prove this. This does not apply only to horses but also to cattle. In western Canada particularly there is a great ranch industry with purebred cattle of all kinds. In order to protect ourselves we have to go to Great Britain to register them and then to the United States. I am fortunate that one of my colleagues is away today and it is my lot to discuss this topic. At one time these matters came under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice and the Secretary of State. I have had some experience in this field.
These are three matters on which the minister can work. Let us get our patents recognized in the United States and Great Britain. Let us get certificates of purebred stock that are recognized outside Canada. Let us have a document that is recognized in the United States, Great Britain and throughout the world. If action were taken to improve the situation in these three areas a great deal of good would be done for the nation. People are constantly complaining about the problem of registering cattle as purebred. I know that this matter comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture but it is very close to the field of patents and trade marks; it is in the same area of law.
I now want to say a few words about the branch of the department that will deal with corporations. It was refreshing to hear the minister discuss this topic so intelligently. This is indeed a big field because, as the minister pointed out, under the British North America Act securities fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government under certain conditions and in other conditions they fall within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
I believe that some of the problems that arose recently in Ontario, as a result of which companies went bankrupt and people lost their

Supply-Registrar General savings-and nobody in particular is to blame for this-were brought about because the provincial and federal officials were not quite sure of the ambit of their jurisdiction. As a result the provincial government waited for the federal government to do something and the federal government waited for the provincial government. Therefore the proposal of the minister is good; it is good philosophy. As I understood the minister-and I made a careful note of what he said and listened carefully to him-the government will work out with the securities commission and the provinces a system similar to that used in Ontario, which everybody recognizes is the soundest in Canada. We should work out a plan, after liaison between the federal government and provincial governments, whereby we can administer securities without there being a conflict of jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, at the adjournment I was speaking about corporations and securities. I said that perhaps the big problem at the time of the collapse of Atlantic Acceptance Corporation and Prudential Finance Corporation was that neither the province nor the federal government appreciated the jurisdictional aspects and nothing was done to warn the people who had placed their savings in those concerns about the economic and financial catastrophe which resulted.
The minister said that he does not want to regulate such concerns and it is true, I think, that most people would agree with him. The minister said that what we need is the kind of regulation that protects the Canadian investor. I am not one of those who go along with the arguments of my hon. friends to my left,

which are sometimes heard not only to my left but also in other parts of the house. When a person wants to invest his money in stocks he must accept the fact that some element of chance is involved. If he is not prepared to take a gamble he must confine his activities to a yield of 4 or 5 per cent in the bond market. But there must be a certain degree of freedom in the investment field so that people are encouraged to invest their money. If the field were too well controlled by the securities commission, you would never be able to change a private company which has certain objects into a public company and sell the stock to the public. Nevertheless, as I say, at the same time the public must be protected.
Before I leave the subject, Mr. Chairman, I dealt earlier in my remarks with the monopoly position that obtains in certain aspects of the work of funeral directors. I should like to put on record, because it is interesting, that preliminary investigation shows that there are 51 firms in Canada making caskets and 8 manufacturing embalming fluid. It is also interesting to note that only one or two firms control the manufacture of hardware for caskets. Therein lies the monopoly.
It is further interesting to note that there is no record of who the directors are of the National Casket Company of Toronto, which is also engaged in the manufacture of embalming fluid and accessories. Neither is there any record of other business details in connection with that company. The National Casket Company of the United States, which has its headquarters in Boston, has no Canadians on the board. Indeed, there is no hint of any Canadian connection. There is no business directory which shows that Mr. McConnell is connected with anything but publishing and sugar. There is a variety of material available, pro and con, in connection with the unnecessary and extremely high cost of funerals, but none of this material is more recent in date than 1960.
I think that this is a field which should be investigated immediately in order to ascertain who controls the casket and embalming fluid manufacturing companies in Canada. This would be, of course, the job of the restrictive trade practices branch. I have always found that when they conduct an investigation they do a very thorough and capable job. They have the kind of personnel we need in this field. I am not ignoring the services of the director of that branch when I say that, but I do know that the men working for him, some of whom have not been trained in the field of
June 16. 1967

law, do an exceptionally good job of investigation and inquiry in relation to preliminary matters which may lead to a prosecution.
1 should like to review one other matter before I go on to another aspect. I pointed out this morning that the statute relating to patents has been so long embalmed that if under its terms a Canadian applies for a patent for an invention and that patent is not registered properly in the United States or in Great Britain, someone else in either of those countries can copy the invention and sell the same thing back to Canada and there is nothing that can be done about it. In effect, it means that a Canadian has to ignore the Canadian statute and make sure that his patent is registered properly in the United States or Great Britain so as to protect his own interests.
I will now turn to the proposed department of consumer affairs. The minister mentioned drugs and the reduction in tax. I think that this problem is very well summed up in an article to which I should like to refer for a moment, because in my opinion drugs are the biggest racket there is. This is an extract from the Albertan for June, 1966:
Your friendly neighbourhood druggist is a spoke- often an unwilling one-in a free-wheeling, sugar-coated racket.
Each day hundreds of thousands of dollars are wrung out of Canadians for badly-needed prescription drugs, and almost without exception the customer shells out from two to ten times as much as he should.
There is a good example here to which I might refer:
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
A German company seized during the war, it was sold to private interests in 1952 for $29,000,000, and chalked up such fat profits that the owners got their investment back in 51 years. During this period the hottest item was an anti-arthritic with the generic name prednisolone. A package of 100 tablets cost the firm $1.57, wholesaled to druggists for $17.90, and retailed at $29.83.
In Calgary. That represented a mark-up of 1,863 per cent.
The same drug was available at the time from a small U.S. generic company at wholesale price of $2.70 per 100.
That was the price they charged instead of $17.90 per hundred.
Words are great. We have our committees and our investigations and they look into this and that and everything else. We want action. The Canadian people are crying for action so far as the drug industry is concerned. Today is the day of pills. That is what people take after going to the doctor. There is a shortage
Supply-Registrar General of doctors, and people are taking pills and drugs. As I say, today is the day of pills. If you have an ache here or an ache there, or a pain in this or that part of your body, pills are prescribed for you. This is the era of drugs. We have advanced far and drugs are helping to keep people healthy. The drug industry knows that this is the age of pills and it has moved into the racket. That is what it is.
We talk about medicare, but the great difficulty these days is not in paying the doctor but in paying the druggist. The doctor may charge you $5 or $10 for an interview but the druggist charges you $25 for the prescription. This is where the problem arises and this is what must be examined and dealt with. The drug industry is a monopoly. In Canada as well as in the United States it has become a racket, and in this country we have only scraped the surface of the problem.
The minister talks about the cost of living, but we must be fair. The Canadian cost of living has been increasing since 1963 and has increased at a much faster rate than at any other time since the war. When we talk of the cost of living we really are talking about consumer credit and the prices consumers must pay, and some of the responsibility for the increase in living costs must be borne by the government.
When the Conservative party formed the government from 1957 to 1962 there was somewhat of a recession in the United States which was reflected in Canada. The leading economists of that time agreed that there was a case for deficit financing. Yet today, when the economies of Canada and the United States are rising and are better than at any time since 1962, we have deficit financing. We have a deficit of $700 million and a new kind of budget. We do not know what would have happened had there been an orthodox budget. When one adds to that deficit the $600 million to be spent on medicare, which is to begin next July, the total deficit will be in the order of $1,100 million.
The minister talks about free enterprise. What is the matter with the country today? Why do we have these combines? Why do we have these monopolies? It is not because the combines investigation people are not doing their job but because governments-not only on the other side of the house but also formed from this side-have been bringing in, beyond the ability of the gross national product of Canada to bear, such grandiose plans that the government spending has necessitated high taxation.
June 16, 1967

Supply-Registrar General
In any small business the greater partner is the government. You cannot tax a small medical clinic, a small legal firm or a small business firm up to 50 per cent of its income and expect it to stay in business and compete with monopolistic groups that have a large turnover for their products. As a result, no matter in which Canadian city you conduct your research you will find the small storekeeper, the small druggist or the small professional man going out of business. I know of a firm of four people which employs a staff of six. Of those six, two are employed to fill out government forms.
Hear, hear.

I hear my left-wing friend saying, "Hear hear." He is happy.
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics sends out forms demanding that they be filled in and returned. Anyone failing to comply with such requests is subject to a fine. Added to that, employers are faced with income tax forms, unemployment insurance forms, pension documents. Two people are needed to fill out forms to take care of every four employees. In the big, automated businesses, machines cope with the demands of bureaucracy, demands which are ever increasing under this government. Small businesses, which have to hire employees to cope with this work, are being driven out of business. That is why we have monopolies. The cost of living is partly the responsibility of this government. The only real new wealth in Canada is not created by the government spending money but is brought about by the creation of capital from the production of goods in the nation.
Hear, hear.

I am glad that my hon. friend from British Columbia agrees with me. He does not always agree with me.
Now I come to the subject of bankruptcy. The minister told us about the new act and about the new set-up in the bankruptcy field. His speech was full of words and fine phrases, but there are other matters that I and other hon. members would have liked to hear about. Has there been any investigation into the group bankruptcies that we have heard about in this country? What about the lawyer, whose name for the moment escapes me, who 18 months or two years ago after investigating bankruptcies was murdered? Has that crime been solved? The Prime Minister talks about syndicated criminals and the bankruptcy racket. What has he done to bring about a solution of the crime?

The house spent some time during the last session of parliament debating capital punishment. The Liberals for once sent their whip home and we had a free vote. We voted against the abolition of capital punishment. I took the position that the government has power to commute and that the government, unless it abuses that privilege, is not flouting the law. Is that privilege to be exercised on behalf of syndicated criminals of the kind who murdered the lawyer or who murdered the 11 people who were discovered buried in lime in the Montreal district? Members of parliament voted to retain capital punishment so that society would have protection against such criminals. There must be some reason for crime to be increasing. The British are reviewing their criminal laws on the subject I spoke of earlier. Why should this matter once again come before this house?
I shall now return to the subject of bankruptcy. I hoped that the minister would give us information. It is true that we have a new act, but that does not mean to say that syndicated criminals in the bankruptcy field will not find ways to enrich themselves at the expense of Canadian business. That sort of thing has been going on for a long time. It is a racket.
