I have only a few minutes to go. I have tried to summar'ze my remarks. I may be the only member from our party to speak on these estimates. We are trying to cut down the number of speeches. The minister may be glad to hear that I believe I am the only speaker from this party-there may be one other. So it is likely the estimates will get through quickly and we can turn to other business.
I was discussing bankruptcy. The former minister of justice, Mr. Cardin, set up a commission of three people to investigate the bankruptcy field. I should like to know what this commission had to say. I should like to have its report summarized for my benefit and for the benefit of the country. I notice
June 16, 1967

there is nobody in the press gallery so perhaps it will never be summarized. When we are absent they mention it, and I do not see why we should not do so when they are absent.
They can hear you upstairs anyway.

That will be very refreshing for them. Bankruptcy is a specialized field and I feel that special courts should be set up to deal with it. There are very few solicitors who understand the law relating to bankruptcy and, as a matter of fact, few judges understand it. In most districts the practice is to appoint one judge with special knowledge in this area and he does 90 per cent of the work. Of the small group of solicitors who understand bankruptcy law, few have knowledge of the criminal law, with the result that it is difficult for them to detect offences under the Criminal Code and prepare charges, when there is evidence of fraud, with the evidence necessary to bring cases before the courts of law.
In summary I maintain, in spite of what the minister has said, that the government has shown little more than a readiness to make regulations and regulate the lives of Canadians. We can point to examples. With regard to the pension plan, for instance, the nine provinces were told: This is what you will get. The former minister, now Secretary of State, told the premier of Alberta: If you don't like it, you will pay for it anyhow and you will not get the benefits. Hon. gentlemen over there are placing business in a strait-jacket as a result of increased bureaucracy and stricter control. They are increasing taxes, already heavy, as an indirect way of socializing business.
I hope, therefore, that when the minister comes to answer some of the questions I have raised he will get away from his beautiful phrases, dust off some facts and let us have some concrete information about the bankruptcy situation. Let him tell us what he is prepared to do with regard to patents. Let him tell us how he proposes to increase liaison between the provinces and his department so far as corporations are concerned. If he keeps these suggestions in mind I think he will be running a very efficient department.
I began on a note of commendation and I meant it. I think we heard this morning a new generation speaking in the House of Commons. I hope I have measured up to my
Supply-Registrar General responsibility by calling to the minister's attention some of the difficulties with which he will have to cope. He is new in this department. Every young man is out to make his name, and I know the hon. gentleman is no exception. He is politically ambitious, and it is no crime to be so. I wish him the best of luck. Maybe next year when the estimates are before us again he will be able to tell us that the patent law of Canada means something to Canadians, will be able to give us a full account as to how the bankruptcy law is operating to clear up crime and a full report on the legislation he has been able to work out with the provinces to control fraud in the selling of stocks and securities so as to protect Canadians who have invested in their nation and who have faith in their nation.

Mr. Chairman, listening to the statement made by the hon. member for Bow River about funerals and embalming I could not help contrasting the morbidity of those remarks with the enlightened observations of the minister, whom I congratulate. The house was certainly left in a different mood. I hope the hon. member for Bow River does not become too confused when he has to look to the right to the left.
I wish to speak about the cost of drugs in Canada, about combines and monopolies, about competition or the lack of it in the drug industry. It is my intention to discuss drug prices in the hope the government can produce legislation which will effectively lower the prices of drugs to Canadian consumers. The hon. member for Bow River made a casual reference to drugs. I intend to devote my entire remarks to that subject and will refer to the studies which were made by the committee and information which I myself have gleaned since the committee last sat. I believe the prices of drugs could be lowered by changing the patent law and by easing compulsory licensing regulations. By way of background I shall seek to explain why the price of drugs is today at such a high level.
It has been stated that drug prices in Canada are the highest in the world. Responsibility for this lies, in my opinion, with a monopolistic group known as the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, referred to as P.M.A.C. for the sake of brevity. This is a combination or combine of 57 drug companies which manufacture 85 per cent of the prescription drugs used in Canada today. They do not compete with each other in price and I like to consider them as a
June 16. 1967

Supply-Registrar General private club to which a manufacturer can belong if his prices are high enough and if he is capable of making a brand name drug with a long name.
This association is monopolistic, as I have said, because there is no competition except in the volume of advertising directed to doctors. Doctors are swamped with advertising material to the tune of $5,000 per year per doctor. Efforts are made to influence them through direct mail advertising amounting to something like a pound of literature a day, most of which is thrown immediately into wastebaskets. The companies use advertising in journals, particularly medical journals including some owned and produced by themselves in which commercials are interspersed with bits of medical information. In addition, gimmicks are given out whose value is difficult to estimate. Certainly they have some value, though no medical information is contained to enable a doctor to decide scientifically which drug he should prescribe for a patient.
I believe-and this was not contradicted in the committee-that there is no direct relationship between the cost of manufacturing a drug and the ultimate selling price to the consumer. I should like to refer to a brief submitted to the special committee on drug costs and prices by the government of Alberta. It was written by Mr. Henry Steele, a professor at the University of Houston, Texas. It is one of the most comprehensive briefs I have ever read. It contains more than a hundred pages and I agree that it is an excellent piece of work. Referring to the Hoffman LaRoche submission to the committee, Mr. Steele states:
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The submission relates that Bell-Craig, in its application for a compulsory licence for chlordia-zepoxide (the so-called "Librium") maintained that while it could not estimate its probable cost of manufacturing the drug very accurately, this was largely irrelevant to the selling price. Roche agreed without comment. The implication is clearly that prices need not be related to costs, and that the cost is so small relative to price that substantial variations in cost would have no significant effect on expected profit margins.
I quote further from the same brief:
Although the "broad-spectrum" antibiotics ail sell at virtually identical prices, production costs appear to differ greatly, at least on the basis of available cost information.
This, Mr. Chairman, certainly proves the point that there is no direct relation between the cost of manufacturing and the ultimate selling price.

When the P.M.A.C. group appeared before our committee I had in my possession at that time a list of 56 drugs with the manufacturers' selling prices to the retail outlet, the drug store, in England, compared with the cost that druggists pay in Ontario for the same drugs, according to the cost book. In this list of 56 drugs there was a differential in price of up to 20 times as much in Canada as in England. One particular drug was sold in Canada at $10 per hundred to druggists, while the same drug sold at 50 cents a hundred to druggists in England. The brand name was the same. The differential had nothing to do with generic manufacturing.
This posed a problem for the P.M.A.C. and their economist took one whole week end to work it out in order to try to give me an answer. In the answer he came up with he lumped together all 56 drugs on my list, not all of them having a price variation of 20 times as much, and devised a factor of the number of hours of work necessary in Canada compared with the number of hours necessary in England to buy this basket of drugs. Then he used this factor, which I believe was 2.4 or 2.04, and multiplied all the English prices by it. This did not bring them quite high enough, so then he went into various other explanations of their system of retail pricing, wholesale pricing, and so on. If we were to accept this explanation, then by the same token I would presume that if I went to India, or any other less developed country, I should be able to purchase a brand new Ford car for about $400, using this line of reasoning. I cannot see that this line of reasoning is acceptable in trying to rationalize the price of drugs in Canada today.
To cite specific examples, Smith, Kline and French is a drug manufacturing company which is a member of this private club. They manufacture a drug known as stelazine, and in 2 mg. size the subsidiary company in Canada was recently purchasing it from the parent company in the United States in dosage form, in other words, in completely manufactured tablets in bulk, all ready for bottling and labelling, at a cost of $1.32 per thousand tablets. These ultimately are sold to the consumer at $6.50 for 50 or $125 for $1,000. I make this out to be a 9,700 per cent markup. I know that labels and bottles are expensive and that pushing drugs is expensive, but I cannot see that a 9,700 per cent mark-up is justified.
I have with me today a book I recently got, printed in 1967, called "The Pill Conspiracy," by George Johnson. It is a very revealing
June 16, 1967	COMMONS
book and should be read by the minister if he is going to do anything at all about drugs. It has been stated that drug prices averaged out only come to double the average profit of over-all industry, which really brings a tear to your eye when you stop to think that the drug manufacturers can only make double the average profit at the expense of sick people.
This book takes individual companies to give a comparison, which is the only fair way of doing it. Based on percentage of sales, which in a sense is not a fair way of estimating profit-it should be figured on dollar investment-this book lists the top 50 industries as individual companies. It shows, for example, that Dupont makes a 22.8 per cent return, General Motors 22.8 per cent and I.B.M. 19.1 per cent. No. 4 on the list, at 35 per cent, was American Home Products Corporation, which owns two or three of our previously Canadian drug manufacturing companies. Smith, Kline and French, which I have just referred to, is No. 6 on the list at 33.9 per cent. All in all, in the top 50 there are six drug companies which are making profits at this level.
To give another example, Mr. Chairman, there is an antibiotic sold by Parke, Davis which, interestingly, is imported from Italy. It would not pay them to manufacture it themselves. They buy it from the very same place in Italy from which they complain we should not buy low quality drugs. They bring it over here, make tablets out of it, bottle, label and sell them. With duty paid the price goes from $1.52 per hundred to $51 per hundred. This leaves quite a bit of leeway too.
I would like to refer to patents in connection with this matter and in particular to Pfizer, a drug manufacturing company which instigated the use of some of our wide-spec-trum antibiotics. This will show what patents tend to do to drug prices. Pfizer's manufacture a drug known as terramycin, whose generic name is oxytetracycline. Its patent on the drug recently expired, something which has happened to very few modem drugs because patents last for 17 years. Pfizer was selling the drug at $16.76 per 100 250 mg. capsules, and here I am taking the liberty of changing shillings and pence into dollars and cents.
About April, 1966, Imperial Chemical Industries started producing and selling oxytetracycline under the trade name imperacin. Its price to druggists for 100 250 mg. capsules was $5.55, one third of Pfizer's price. Since then Pfizer's price has dropped from $16.76 to $12.58. It must not be forgotten that Pfizer had the advantage of having the market for a
DEBATES	1617
Supply-Registrar General period of 17 years and was known as the manufacturer of oxytetracycline.
In addition, these companies are protected by antiquated patent laws and patents which apply to the processing in Canada and by anti-dumping duties, prior to the budget earlier this month, which were based on class or kind imported into Canada. As I understand it, the word "class" has been eliminated and the duty is based now on kind only.
Manufacturers have a great deal of difficulty in acquiring a compulsory licence, and the initiator of a drug also has the advantage of new drug status for five years. There has been an actual example in history of a company which, having a compulsory licence applied for against it, in turn applied to be reinstated on a new drug status in order to protect itself against having a compulsory licence granted whereby another company could manufacture its drug. The idea of new drug status is to keep a drug under the control of the initial manufacturer so that any side effects can be reported and the food and drug directorate can take steps to remove the drug from the market, or whatever the case may be.
In order to ensure that drugs sell well and that the doctors are properly brainwashed by the brand name companies, these companies send detail men to doctors' offices in order to push the sale of their drugs. They do not really teach a doctor anything except the advantage of the taste of a drug, its colour, its size, and the brevity of the name of the drug they are pushing. Their second purpose is to disparage the use of generic drugs. They do not do this openly or overtly but nevertheless they give the doctor the feeling that any generic drug is second rate. The suggestion is that the doctor would not want to give his patient a second rate drug. Because doctors are very busy they are very vulnerable to such propaganda. It is easy to remember a trade name, and the doctor does not do the purchasing. The purchasing is done by the patient, so the price is of no real concern to the doctor.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
At the same time the drug manufacturers, through the detail men, are providing the only form of continuing education that the doctors receive. The detail man brings the drug and the information right into the doctor's office. He brainwashes the doctor. He tells him that the only drug he should use is the one from his company. He does not tell the doctor anything about price nor does he suggest a price which should form the basis for competition. This leaves the doctor in the
June 16. 1967

Supply-Registrar General position of being the agent of the drug manufacturers. He does not buy the drug himself but he receives the advantages, if any, of all the advertising and all the gimmicks. Yet it is the patient who spends the money.
I should like to refer again to the book known as "The Pill Conspiracy" in order to read two paragraphs which appear at page 156:
The American companies took an intense interest in how the Italians could sell tetracycline anywhere near as good as the domestic brands for as little as $1.43 per one hundred.
The American Cyanamid Co., parent of Lederle Laboratories, soon discovered that some Italian brands were not almost as good, they were precisely as good-because they were precise copies of its patented product. It had no legal recourse in Italy, which has no patent laws, so it started investigating to find out how the Italians obtained the mold cultures and production knowledge essential to duplicating achromycin.
This is the trade name under which they sell tetracycline.
In a recent issue of the AFL-CIO News of May 13 there is an article by Sidney Mar-golius. One sentence reads as follows:
The F.D.A.-
The food and drug directorate in the United States.
-pilot study reports that 7.7 per cent of drugs sold under generic names, which it had tested, and 8.8 per cent of those sold under brand names failed to meet acceptable potency standards.
In other words, 8.8 per cent of the brand name drugs were unacceptable and 7.7 per cent were unacceptable among the disparaged generic names which it is suggested it is inadvisable for the doctor to prescribe. These companies have a great deal of difficulty acquiring a compulsory licence. They cannot obtain a compulsory licence on imported manufactured products. Basically the price is much less.
There is another example involving a tranquillizer. We seem to be in an era of tranquillizers. If you are not in it you are not taking tranquillizers. Equanil, which is the brand name for meprobamate, sells to the patient for approximately $10 per 100. The brand name drug is purchasable for $6 per 1,000. Tetracycline here in Ottawa-and I made inquiries to ascertain this-can be purchased by the druggist for $2.50 per 100 whereas the previous price he was paying was $18 per 100.
There is a problem here in respect of drugs which are prescribed by a doctor in their generic form, because the druggist is able to dispense either the brand name drug or the 
generic name drug. If he is going to make 40 per cent on the sale, it naturally will pay him to dispense the most expensive drug he has. It has been my suggestion-there are drug stores across Canada which are doing this -that druggists should dispense on a cost plus a professional fee basis. I realize that this will make the very cheap drug a little more expensive for the patient but it will make the more expensive drug much cheaper and will stop the temptation of the retail druggist to dispense the most expensive brand he has in his store.
I should like to refer again to the book "The Pill Conspiracy":
McKesson & Robbins put its generic tetracycline on the market at $6 per one hundred capsules- compared to $17.60 for the brand names-and the pharmacists of America promptly provided the public with an education as to their pricing practices.
They had been selling the brand names at about $5.70 for 16, for a profit of almost exactly 100 per cent. When McKesson & Robbins cut the wholesale price 66 per cent the pharmacies reduced the retail price to $4.40 for 16, increasing their profit to almost 460 per cent!
So one can see the advantage of what I have just said. It is acutely necessary that druggists get into the habit of dispensing on the basis of cost plus a dispensing fee. I should like to cite one more example from this book:
Senator Long found an even wider spread between the public and government prices for a reserpine brand named serpasil. As serpasil, he said, it cost the druggist $39.50 per one thousand. As reserpine, it costs the government 47 cents per one thousand. The cost to the patient is about $65, versus 47 cents that the government pays.
This is a large price spread. I do not see how the minister can do other than agree that there is a monopoly, a combine and almost everything there should not be so far as the P.M.A.C. group of manufacturers in this country are concerned.
Dr. Chapman, the director of the food and drug directorate of Canada, appeared before the committee and made the statement that generic drugs basically are just as good as name brand drugs. They have the protection of the new drug standards. The brand name companies maintain that if it is a brand name drug this means it is a quality drug. I suggest that the brand name does not mean quality. It is not a synonymous term. Quality is determined by how the drug is manufactured and not by the name which appears on the label or how pretty the bottle is.
June 16. 1967	COMMONS
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
There is one way that people can do something about lowering drug prices and that is by shopping for their prescriptions at various retail outlets. They will find a considerable difference in drug mark-ups at discount stores as a result of volume sales. The patient can also go to the doctor and ask for the generic name. The patient really has just one choice when he shops and that is the store to which he goes. If you go to buy a loaf of bread or a can of vegetables from a store you have two choices. You can go to whichever store you like and you can buy whichever brand you want, realizing that they are all expensive. In any event you have a double choice. With a prescription you have only one choice and that is as to which friendly neighbourhood drug store you take your prescription.
This means that we have a powerful moneyed group which is subsidized by the sick and partly by the doctors who are writing prescriptions because of the pressure exerted by this monopoly group. The expense of research is subsidized by the sick who can afford it the least.
I found out to my amazement that the P.M.A.C. did not like some of the things I have been saying, and I have proof of this fact in a letter I received about a month ago from the president of the P.M.A.C. I should like to put it on the record in sections and comment on them. It is from Dr. W. W. Wi-gle. Dr. Wigle was previously the president of the Canadian Medical Association and he was hired to try to add an air of decency to the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association. He starts off by saying:
Dear Dr. Howe:
As a physician I am amazed at the interpretation of your remarks printed in the Ottawa papers recently.
He referred to the interpretation of my remarks. Actually I said these things and there was no interpretation necessary. Today I believe I have made my point very clear so there is no need to interpret any of my remarks. They can be reported verbatim. The letter continues:
Having presented factual evidence to the parliamentary committee on which you served that the manufacturer's portion of the prescription dollar is 37J per cent I cannot imagine how a reporter would get the impression that a reduction (or the complete elimination) of the manufacturer's portion could reduce the price by 75 per cent. We quoted from figures supplied by the pharmacists' association, not the P.M.A.C.
I made the statement that drug prices could be lowered by 75 per cent, but this outfit has
DEBATES	1619
Supply-Registrar General the ability to twist figures around to make it look as though it is a charitable institution and that only 37| cents could be taken off the drug dollar. But it does not stop to think or purposely avoids stating that there are different kinds of dollars. I would be very willing to let these people have 37\ per cent of my drug dollar but it would be a great deal less than the one they have in mind. Perhaps they should have 40 per cent of my dollar if they need the money, but each dollar would be a lot smaller and there would be fewer of them.
Government offices invariably purchase drugs from drug manufacturers on a tender basis and almost invariably they buy generic drugs. If drug stores were to work on a Canadian formulary basis under which drug companies submitted tenders to the drug stores it would be amazing how far the 100 per cent they have in mind would drop. In some cases it would drop to 10 per cent. In this way drugs would reach the drug stores much more cheaply and the stores would only have to carry one brand. This would eliminate about 30 per cent now being spent on the advertising done by the drug companies.
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has now expired.
Carry on.
Does the hon. gentleman have the unanimous consent of the committee to continue?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman and hon. members. I will not take too much longer and I did not realize I had already taken so much time.
As I was saying, if a formulary basis were adopted and drug stores had the choice of buying any one of a number of brand products which were all equal, the quality having been determined by the food and drug directorate of Canada, with the elimination of the need for the space to store 20 different brands and the elimination of the 30 cents of the prescription dollar spent on advertising directed to the doctors, I am sure drug prices could be reduced by 75 per cent. I disagree with these distorted figures of the P.M.A.C.
The next paragraph of this letter reads as follows:
I wonder if the thousands of dollars (and the thousands of hours of work) spent by our industry in preparing information for your committee was all
June 16, 1967

Supply-Registrar General in vain. Did it fall on deaf ears? Do you accuse us of lying? It is impossible for me to understand your refusal to accept documented evidence.
Of the 37| cents of each dollar that they claim to spend on drug research, only 2 J cents is actually spent on research, with 11J cents being spent for promotion. As a result of all the money they claim they spend on research, there has not been a breakthrough in research in Canada in the last 15 years. Research in Canada is very small, even taking into account all the drug manufacturers and all the P.M.A.C. group, including the parent companies of all the subsidiaries. What these drug companies do is combine drugs and give them a different name. This gives them a new drug status and they are protected from compulsory licences for another five years.
Another thing these companies do is what is called molecular manipulation. They make a slight change in a product, possibly an antibiotic, and give it a different name. As a result they obtain a new patent which is good for another 17 years. This is the sort of thing they claim is costing so much money. They suggest that 2J cents per drug dollar represents millions of dollars spent on research. That being the case, imagine how much is spent on promotion if 11J cents per dollar is used for that purpose.
The last paragraph of this letter was of great interest to me. It states:
If your actions are designed to appeal to the voter, I wish you luck. If they are designed to increase your acceptability as a physician and scientist I doubt that you have impressed your colleagues in practice or academic circles or in industry.
I do not know whether that has any political connotations, but I am glad that he wishes me luck. The articles were published in Ottawa, not in Hamilton where my voters are. Is Dr. Wigle trying to say that my medical practice is going to be jeopardized in the future because I have spoken out frankly in an attempt to convey to the people of Canada the facts about the drug manufacturing hoax which exists in this country today? With particular reference to the brand name companies operating under the protective shield of the P.M.A.C., if what I said before was an attempt to solicit votes Dr. Wigle can certainly accuse me of this again because of what I have said today with greater emphasis.
I believe the government can reduce the cost of drugs by establishing compulsory licensing, particularly in respect of the importation of drugs. That was the basis of a recommendation of the committee. This would

inject competition into the industry. At this time there is no competition among members of the P.M.A.C. and there is no competition outside that organization. A monopoly is being operated and these companies are thriving. How can you rationalize a 9,700 per cent mark-up? How can you rationalize the government buying something for 27 cents which is sold at 100 times that much to private individuals?
I believe that Canadians, particularly sick people, deserve protection from this form of profiteering. The sicker a person is, the more drugs and money he needs. The more drugs he needs, the less he can afford them and the less he can afford to pay for this terrible profiteering. The drug manufacturers have perpetrated on the doctors of this country a brainwashing job to convince them to prescribe their drugs so they can continue to make for themselves and their shareholders an immense profit. The only way we can lower the price of drugs in Canada is to inject competition into the industry. I ask the government sincerely to do something to solve this serious problem. The minister spoke with all sorts of idealistic terminology, which I appreciate. However, if there is any sincerity in this regard something must be done to lower the price of drugs, and I think that this can be done by legislation.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, in rising to participate briefly in this debate I want to say through you, sir, to the minister that he has perhaps more than any other minister a great responsibility in his department and the branches assigned to his ministry in improving and maintaining the free, competitive economic system that we have in Canada. He has, as has been pointed out, under his jurisdiction the Bankruptcy Act, the Combines Investigation Act, the corporations branch and the patents branch. Taking all these together, there are probably more abusive practices in the free, competitive economic system which can be dealt with by one or other of these branches than by any other department of government. I hope the minister realizes the tremendous responsibility that he has to see that these abuses are dealt with as they arise, so that we can maintain the kind of economic system that many of us in this house as well as throughout the country value so highly.
I shall speak only very briefly on one aspect of these estimates. It is one that has been discussed quite a lot this afternoon. I refer to
June 16. 1967

drugs and the monopoly that many of us believe exists in this industry. Whether it is a monopoly, a combine or whatever makes no difference; the fact is that the result, in our opinion, is a far higher price structure at the consumer level than is necessary. The main question I want to pose to the minister this afternoon is: Why do we not take some action in respect of the many recommendations that have been made, not only by members of this house but by competent firms which have been retained by the governments of many provinces to carry out studies in this area?
There is no lack of evidence before this house in the form of findings and recommendations with regard to what the government ought to do and what action it ought to take to change some of our laws and effect a lowering of drug prices. We have, as the hon. member for Hamilton South pointed out, the submission of the government of Alberta which I think was excellent, although I was at the committee for only a limited number of hearings. The hon. member for Hamilton South was a member of the committee during all its hearings.
A large number of those recommendations were accepted by the committee and included in their report. That report has been before the government for quite a long time. We appreciate that when bringing down the budget the Minister of Finance announced he was going to remove the 12 per cent sales tax on drugs. He also mentioned that some of his colleagues would be introducing legislation to take care of some of the other recommendations. So far that is all we have. I should like the minister to know that his announcement has not changed the price of drugs very much. In fact, it has not changed the price of drugs at all. The fact is, if the rumours we hear are true, that it has increased the price of drugs until September 1, and they were too high before. I should like to refer the minister to one paragraph of the report of the committee; which can be found in Votes and Proceedings at page 1641:
Both the drug manufacturers and retail pharmacists offered the opinion before the committee that the benefits of a reduction in sales tax would be passed along to the consumer.
What a hope. However, Mr. Chairman, the committee was not quite as naive as would appear from that statement. The report says further:
However, the committee concludes that, without more effective operation of competitive forces than presently exists in the drug industry in Canada, the only certain result from removal of the tax would be a reduction in costs to the manufacturers.
Supply-Registrar General
What appears to have happened thus far is that rather than reducing the price by 12 per cent even at the manufacturers' level, the pharmacists and manufacturers have indicated that there might be an 8 per cent reduction or maybe a 5 per cent reduction in price. But they do not define on what that reduction will be based. Will it be on the basis of the prices that prevailed prior to the minister's statement in the house or will it be based on the prices in effect on September 1 when the sales tax will be removed? It certainly does not add up to very much benefit to the consumer if between June 1, when the Minister of Finance brought down his budget, and September 1-a period of three months-they raise the price by as much as they intend reducing it. There is, therefore, no reduction at all to the consumer.
I wonder whether the minister and his department are taking into account what the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association, and perhaps even the local pharmacists, are doing to the price of drugs in the intervening period. It seems to me to be most unfair that we should give the local pharmacists, and perhaps the wholesale distributors of drugs, a three months' period to protect themselves against a loss in the value of their inventory, if they are allowed to nullify the minister's intention in this way. In my opinion this is not keeping faith with the intent of the minister's announcement and it is certainly not doing what is just.
The Minister of Finance could have reduced the price of drugs by withdrawing the sales tax at once, effective June 1 when he made the statement. But he did not. The reason he gave for not doing so was to allow a period in which the drug manufacturers could protect the value of their inventories. Now they are flying right in the face of that very reasonable action and are in the meantime raising their prices. The net price after September 1 will be no lower than it is today. In my opinion this is a disgraceful attitude for the pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors to take. It seems to me it is not in keeping with the spirit or intent of the minister's announcement.
I intended to deal at some length with the summary of recommendations of the government of the province of Alberta, which is to be found in chapter V of their brief. I also intended to deal with the recommendations of the committee which can be found at page 1664 of Votes and Proceedings. However, the hon. member for Hamilton South has dealt
June 16, 1967

Supply-Registrar General with that matter and pressed for action in this regard. Therefore all I wish to say is that we believe we need action, and it is within the jurisdiction of this minister to take action, in respect of such things as compulsory licences for the importation of drugs. There is also the matter of the Patent Act. Amendments should be introduced so that the burden of proof in respect of any infringement of drug prices and patents would be on the plaintiif. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-4, concerning reform of the bail system.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to reform and improve the bail system of Canada. As is set forth in the explanatory notes of the bill, the measure aims-
-to asure that all persons, regardless of their financial status, shall not needlessly be detained pending their appearance to answer charges under acts of the Parliament of Canada, when detention serves neither the ends of justice nor the public interest.
This measure will permit poor people awaiting trial to be released without bond and will thus eliminate the arbitrary cruelty in the present bail system.
The no-bail release system established by this bill is limited to instances where the offence is not punishable by death or life imprisonment and in which the judge deems the defendant trustworthy.
The bill will also assure that persons convicted of crimes and infractions will receive credit for time spent in custody prior to trial against service of any sentence imposed by the court.
I intend to outline very briefly the detailed amendments proposed to the Criminal Code in line with the aim of this bill and also in line with the safeguarding of the powers of the court to compel the appearance of an accused. First however I would like to remind hon. members that the bill follows almost precisely the trail blazed last year in the United States when the President signed similar legislation into effect with these words:
It is a move to ensure that defendants are considered as individuals and not as dollar signs.
That our Canadian scales of justice are sometimes weighted not with mercy but with money has been apparent in the matter of before trial detention. A very detailed study of the situation was made in 1965 by M. L. Friedland of the faculty of law of the University of Toronto. I should like to quote briefly from the writings of Mr. Friedland. This is what he wrote:
In the setting of bail there is an undue preoccupation with its monetary aspects. The tragedy is that a large percentage of persons are unable to raise the bail that is set (two-thirds according to the Toronto study). The ability of the accused to marshal funds or property in advance determines whether he will be released and may have an effect on the outcome of his case.
The professional bondsmen and moneylenders operate more or less openly, and in my
Bail Reform
opinion their operations are open to criticism. Actually, the system does not do too much to ensure the appearance of the accused in court, and the people who lend the money reap substantial profits. Some accused, in order to raise the money, commit further offences while awaiting trial. The system tends to favour the professional criminal, who is more likely to know and be trusted by the professional bondsmen.
It seems to me that here is a field which requires reform. I would say that if money rather than character is not to determine justice, the accused should be released, if he is to be released at all, on his own recognizance, or, in appropriate cases, with recognizances by sureties in reasonable amounts recoverable if the accused fails to appear.
The bill which I am proposing as a means to meet and reform the existing bail system would make these specific changes in the Criminal Code, and I quote from the text of the bill:
...any person charged with an offence under an Act of the Parliament of Canada, other than an offence punishable by death or imprisonment for life, shall at his appearance in court, be ordered released pending trial on his personal recognizance or upon the execution of an unsecured appearance bond in an amount specified by the court, unless the judge determines, in the exercise of his discretion, that such a release will not reasonably assure the appearance of the person as required.
3. (1) When a judge makes such a determination, he shall, either in lieu of or in addition to the methods of release referred to in section 2, impose the first of the following conditions of release which will reasonably assure the appearance of the person for trial or, if no single condition gives that assurance, any of the combination of the following conditions:
(a)	place the person in the custody of a designated person or organization agreeing to supervise him;
(b)	place restrictions on the travel, association, or place of abode of the person during the period of release;
(c)	require the execution of an appearance bond in a specified amount and the deposit in the registry of the court, in cash or other security as directed, of a sum not to exceed 10 per centum of the amount of the bond, such deposit to be returned upon the performance of the conditions of release;
(d)	require the execution of a bail bond with sufficient solvent sureties, or the deposit of cash in lieu thereof; or
(e)	impose any other condition deemed reasonably necessary to assure appearance as required, including a condition requiring that the person return to custody after specified hours.
Clause 4 of the bill reads:
Any time spent in custody at the prison, penitentiary, reformatory or jail previous to the pronouncing of the sentence shall be credited to any person convicted of an offence.

I believe, and I hope that hon. members will agree, that the proposed legislation gives the magistrate of the court adequate discretionary powers and powers to compel the appearance of the accused, while at the same time providing greater authority than is now the case for the court to judge the character rather than the money of the accused, in determining justice.
In conclusion I will say that failure to raise money should not be the reason for an accused remaining in custody. Deterrents against absconding should be vigilance of search, certainty of recapture and prosecution. It is my hope that the bill may find support and that hon. members may find sufficient merit in the subject matter of this proposal to refer it for more detailed discussion to the appropriate committee of the house, which might be the committee on justice and legal affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-4 raises the question which has been in the minds of many lawyers and legislators for some time, about the justice of the bail system in this country. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) referred to this problem in some detail during the debate on the speech from the throne at the beginning of this session, and I am glad to see that the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill has taken up the challenge and has made a proposal to the house which will perhaps encourage early attention to this matter by the government.
The speech from the throne indicated that amendments to the Criminal Code would be proposed during this session. I hope that provisions relating to release pending trial

will be part of these changes. The objectives sought by this bill can perhaps be accomplished largely, if not entirely, by amendment to the Criminal Code. It seems unnecessary to pass a separate bill, such as this one proposed by the hon. member. It is the practice under the Criminal Code in many areas of Canada, which is not as flexible as the hon. member would like nor as most commentators on this problem would like. The bill before the house, however, emphasises the desirability of release pending trial, and to this extent I think the bill serves a very useful purpose.
The Criminal Code is based on the principles of English law which recognize that, as a general rule, a person should retain his freedom pending a decision on any charge made against him. The author of the report to which my hon. friend referred. Professor M. L. Friedland of the University of Toronto, in a speech delivered to the John Howard Society of Kingston on February 22, 1966, pointed out that the concept of bail which he advocated is the one envisaged by the Criminal Code and the one presently in operation in England. Professor Friedland claimed that the practice in the administration of justice in the province of Ontario, or at least in Toronto where his study was undertaken, was "an undesirable and unjustified gloss on the traditional concept of bail". It may be, therefore, that little change in the Criminal Code is required and that what is required is extensive change in the practice of the local authorities in applying the terms of the Criminal Code.
I think that the hon. member who sponsored this bill did not go as far as the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) went, because as reported at page 306 of Hansard for May 16 last there is a recommendation by the hon. member for Rosedale in these terms:
My recommendation, therefore, is that the provisions of the Criminal Code requiring that an accused person be taken into custody for a broad spectrum of offences should be sharply curtailed and that many offences should he exempted from the necessity of custody and therefore of bail.
What the sponsor of this bill does attempt to do is to put the emphasis on the release of prisoners rather than on their detention. The general effect of the present sections of the Criminal Code is that the court may release an accused on bail on his own recognizance with or without a deposit or with or without sureties. Aside from the special case of offences punishable by death or life imprisonment, the proposed bill would make it the general rule that an accused must be released without
June 16. 1967

having to find sureties or deposit money. Second, the conditions under which sureties, cash deposits or other restrictions could be imposed would be limited to the case where the judge considers that release without bail will not assure attendance of the accused at trial.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, there have undoubtedly been abuses under the present system. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Rosedale and by Professor Friedland that in far too many cases, certainly in the Toronto area and I assume elsewhere in Canada, proceedings under the Criminal Code too often are commenced by arrest rather than by summons.
In a submission to the Canadian Committee on Corrections the John Howard Society had this to say:
The practice of allowing bail is obviously to put the accused at the least inconvience until his guilt or innocence is established. However, there is a crucial problem related to the establishing of the amount of bail. A bank robber might be willing to forfeit a large amount put up through the receipts of his crime whereas a $50 bond may be an impossibility for a maried man on a low income. Thus the poor, the homeless and the friendless may be discriminated against. If unable to face the economic and social distress of incarceration while awaiting trial the accused may borrow money for bail which might leave him v/ithout funds to retain a lawyer, putting him at an immediate disadvantage in court.
The Society recommends: a much broader use of an accused's own recognizance; bail set at a minimum amount consistent with the likelihood of his appearing in court; consideration of the accused's economic situation in determining bail; use of bailbondsmen to be discouraged as the part payment put up by the accused is probably sufficient in itself; the establishment of an investigation bureau in large metropolitan areas, where the accused is not likely to be well known, to establish quickly his economic position.
Similar recommendations were made by the John Howard Society to the McRuer royal commission inquiry into civil rights in Ontario. In the Society's brief to the McRuer commission it said it might be argued that the practice with respect to bail negates the presumption of innocence until proven guilty, or to the contrary, that it supports this presumption by placing the defendant at the least inconvenience until he is proven guilty. The considerations which determine the granting of bail and the amount of surety should be based upon the probability that the defendant will appear in court to face trial, that he will not commit other offences while at liberty, that he will not intimidate witnesses and that he will not remove or destroy evidence. I Suggest that all of these purposes can be
Bail Reform
served without resort to the practice that has been so common, particularly in the Toronto area, of placing undue emphasis on money as the basis for release from custody.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Professor Friedland, in speaking to the John Howard Society of Kingston said that detention before trial had been one of the most neglected areas in the whole administration of criminal justice. He pointed out that questions concerning bail and custody arise only where the accused is arrested rather than summonsed. He reported that the overwhelming majority of accused persons in Toronto who had been charged with criminal offences were arrested rather than summonsed. The authorities in Toronto have attempted to correct this situation, but perhaps an amendment to the Criminal Code along the lines suggested by the sponsor of the bill and the hon. member for Rosedale would encourage that process of reform.
I think that the sponsor's proposal, for the committee on justice and legal affairs to study this problem, is reasonable. There should be an examination of the other side of the coin. The association of police chiefs should be given an opportunity to make representations to members of parliament so that the difficulties, as seen by the police, can be explored. Members of the legal profession and other interested groups should be given an opportunity to express their opinions. It seems to me that this problem ought to be attacked by parliament in this session if possible, and when changes are introduced in the Criminal Code I hope that bail will be one of the subjects of change.
I wish to quote briefly from an editorial in the Toronto Daily Star of April 28, 1967, which seems to put the problem as well as I have seen it put by any speaker or writer. In saying what it did the Star referred to something which affected constituents of mine. It said:
The futility of the bail system in Canadian courts was perfectly illustrated by the case of James Royal here this week.
Royal was charged with rape, and committed for trial in the Supreme Court. Bail was fixed at $3,000. A friend of Royal's persuaded a Scarborough couple to post it for him, although they did not know the accused.
Royal failed to appear for trial, and has apparently left the province. His bail was accordingly forfeited. Chief Justice Gale reduced the forfeiture, but the Scarborough couple will still have to pay $2,000.
What purpose did this whole procedure serve?

June 16, 1967
Bail Reform
The posting of $3,000 did not prevent Royal from fleeing the jurisdiction. It will not make it any easier to track him down and arrest him.
The only effect has been to subject a couple, whose sole offence was to be too trusting, to a heavy penalty.
Yet at the same time many people who are charged with much less serious offences and who have no intention or likelihood of fleeing to escape trial, are kept in jail, sometimes for months, because they or their relatives cannot raise the required cash or property bail.
Would it not be simpler and better, when a man is committed for trial, for the magistrate to consider whether he can safely release the defendant on his own recognizance-that is, on his undertaking to appear before the court on the day set?
In the majority of cases, release on these terms would be quite safe. The average defendant, especially if he has a job and family, is not likely to take to flight and become a fugitive from justice for the rest of his life.
There are instances where, because of the extreme seriousness of the charge, or the defendant's past record, or for some other reason, there is real cause to fear that he will skip out.
In that case it may be necessary to keep him in jail until the trial. In the James Royal case, for example, it might have been wiser to keep the accused behind bars.
But, the decision to hold or release the accused should be based on the circumstances of the case and the man's position and reputation-not, as it is now, or whether he can raise a specified amount of money or persuade someone else to put it up for him.
The presence or absence of a bail bond, we suspect, has little or no effect on a defendant's decision to stay or run away.
The bail system, in fact, is one of those medieval survivals which encumber our courts, and which make no sense under modern conditions.
The time is overdue to eliminate it.
The sponsor of the bill has performed a service in bringing this matter to the floor of the house, and the hon. member for Rosedale has contributed much to the consideration of the problem. I think that the committee on justice and legal affairs should have an opportunity to consider it and I hope that the Minister of Justice will see to it that the committee has that opportunity.
I hope, too, that we shall see an amendment to the Criminal Code later in this session, and that the ideas contained in the present bill as well as those ideas that are contained in the remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale, the suggestions made by the John Howard Society and those of Professor Friedland will be considered in framing a more liberal Criminal Code which better reflects the traditions of British justice than does our present code, and the practice under it, in Canada.

What is $5,000 a year to anyone receiving the salary he receives, or received in the past?
There is also John Doyle who was found guilty in the United States of a fraud against the securities laws of an American state. He came back to Canada, to Newfoundland, where he is free and beyond interference. He engages from time to time in political "fixing" about which I can go into detail if anybody wants information on the subject. But there he sits, a respected financier who owed the Canadian government literally millions of dollars in income tax according to the Department of National Revenue, back in our midst living the life of a respected gentleman
June 16, 1967

because he was able to secure bail following his conviction.
Too often the possession of great riches or the ability to put up a large amount of bail places certain people in an advantageous position while the poor must remain in custody. There are various cases to which reference can be made. I can think of one in the last few weeks. The hon. member who preceded me mentioned Toronto. I do not think Toronto is in any different position because, after all, Toronto has rightly earned the description "Toronto the Good"; that is what it was called in my boyhood days in the east of the city, and no one wants to take away that description today. What the hon. member has described as taking place in Toronto takes place in other parts of the country.
I would respectfully suggest that this bill should not be talked out, and I will not contribute to that occurrence. I believe it should be passed with one qualification-that it should be examined carefully in committee in the manner proposed by the hon. member for York-Sear borough (Mr. Stanbury): Every discretion is left to the judge or the magistrate before whom an application for bail is made in order that the appearance of the person concerned may be assured. We should not allow poverty to be a passport to prison even for a matter of months prior to trial.
The judge has wide discretion. The safeguards are here. The trend in criminology today is not to imprison in cases where it is possible to be reasonably assured, following a first offence, that the ends of justice will be met without the imposition of imprisonment. No one should be sent to prison for any period of time if the judge before whom an application for bail is made can be given a reasonable assurance that the person concerned will turn up for trial.
I say to the hon. member who introduced this bill that strong criticism can be levelled against all of us for not having brought about years ago the implementation of the plan he presents. There may be shortcomings in certain parts of it; there may be alterations which should be made. But the principle deserves to be accepted, and that is what second reading is for. I give my unequivocal support to the purpose, the objective and the general idea which is inherent in this bill and I hope that the house once and for all will show that private members' bills shall not be subject to the guillotine, in a round about manner, by being talked out when they have in them so much to commend as has this bill before us.
Bail Reform
The hon. member for York-Scarborough has made a perfect case for this bill and I feel sure he must have been speaking for the Liberal party in what he had to say. This matter should not be left in a state of suspended animation; it is something which deserves the support of all. It is above political considerations. Bail is granted in all types of cases. I have had bail granted in murder cases when the judge concluded that the evidence at a preliminary hearing was not of such a compelling nature that there was a full and complete case made out. The bail was quite small, as a matter of fact-$5,000. It could have been raised in the two cases to which I referred earlier, but very often bail of even $50 is too much to impose.
No matter whether an individual is acquitted thereafter or not, the fact that he was kept in jail before his trial leaves on him a stigma which remains for years. I ask for support for this bill and at the same time I add once more my appreciation to the hon. member for having brought forward a measure which deserves general support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to add a few comments about that interesting bill introduced in the house by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather).
I am very happy that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) agreed to say a few words about that matter, in view of the fact that he said that it had been a long time since he had last taken part in a debate on private members' hour, and all the more so since his reputation as a criminal lawyer is very well known.
However, Mr. Speaker, I do not fully agree with the Leader of the Opposition when he says that since the bill is proposed on private members' hour, it should necessarily be passed by the house. I have too often heard him say that a matter should be studied very closely before being approved by the house, to agree with him that after an hour's discussion a bill proposed by an hon. member should necessarily be passed.
Even if I sincerely commend the hon. member for New Westminster for having submitted to the house this bill whose object is to correct abuses in the legal field, I have to confess that it does not come up completely to my idea of the amendments which should be made to existing legislation, and especially the Criminal Code as far as the release of the accused until the end of his trial is concerned.

June 16, 1967
Bail Reform
In my opinion, this bill originates from natural laws for the prevention of abuses, but it leaves everything to arbitrary action, and too much has been left to discretion for too long. I take the liberty to draw from the vast experience I acquired in the practise of my profession since I had the opportunity to act as assistant attorney general for the province of Quebec, in Montreal, for some time.
Even though I performed those duties for only a short time, that is, for two years, I realized that some provisions in this act concerning the release of accused persons had to be changed.
First of all, I am willing to admit that an accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty by the court, that such person must necessarily enjoy all the advantages of his innocence and, thus, of his freedom, whenever possible.
Let me summarize briefly the present bail system. A person may be released pending the conclusion of the court proceedings either on his own recognizance or on a personal bail for a certain amount, or on bail supplied by a third party on real or personal property, or on a personal bond or a bond supplied by a third party.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Doubtless much could be added, could be said on the matter, but my time is rather limited. I should like to mention however, that bail, considering present-day progress, should be related, first, to the cost of prosecution and next, to the compensation awarded the victim or victims of the offence.
Police work and communications systems being as perfected as they are, Mr. Speaker, I do not think the accused stands a chance of getting away and evading the due processes of law. But, and this is very important, should it happen, costs incurred by the Crown or by the person suing privately should be guaranteed, up to a point, and the victim or victims should receive compensation if the accused were to disappear. Therefore, I suggest that those are the two major considerations on the basis of which bail should be set.
In view of the fact that the costs of prosecution are not very high, I fail to see clearly why bails of $10,000 or $15,000 should be granted, unless it is necessary to pay compensation to the victim. In such a case, the amount involved should be much larger.
The setting of a $20,000 bail to prevent people from getting away is, in my opinion, something which should not be taken into

consideration nowadays, especially when you consider that there are several bills on the order paper to the effect that compensation should be paid to the victims of criminal attempts or offences. A solution to the problem would be that, if a person disappears, the bail money be given to the victim as compensation and to cover the costs of the crown or the fees of the private prosecutor.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the last few days, during a meeting of the commission of inquiry into the administration of justice in Quebec, I said that the Human Rights League had submitted an interesting brief, recommending that justices of the peace be appointed for a judicial district or districts, in order to receive information, hold hearings, adjourn proceedings and grant bail. These justices of the peace could arrange their sittings in such a way that a person could be set free on bail at any time of the day and on any day of the week.
The same brief-I am speaking of the Human Rights League because this is recent-mentioned the case of a lawyer who had to make eight or ten telephone calls before he was able to reach a judge at 11 o'clock at night to have someone freed on bail.
I often had the same experience myself when, at nine or ten at night, I had to make telephone calls to find a judge with the necessary competence to grant a $50 bail to a person who, for example, had been arrested, say, for speeding.
I have always thought that it was unfair and inconsistent with the spirit of the law. Now, if the Criminal Code were amended to enable the judge to sit during the night or at any time, that would help to solve the problem, but it would still be better to determine the granting of bails in advance through an amendment to the Criminal Code. Otherwise, I do not see how this problem can be solved.
The fact of having ten statutes conflicting with the Criminal Code is inconsistent with the spirit of the law, especially from the practical point of view. It would be advisable, for any minor violation, to determine the penalty for a warrant of arrest. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, that amount could be determined according to the seriousness of the violation as well as the above-mentioned considerations and proportionately to the costs of the proceedings and the compensation of the victim of an offence. In this way, it would not be necessary to disturb a judge at 11 o'clock at night or to make ten telephone calls to set up
June IS, 1967

a $50 bail and release the accused. When it is impossible to reach a judge, or when the person arrested does not have the means to retain the services of counsel, he spends the night in jail, quite often even the whole week.
I have found by experience that this happens regularly. We must be practical. I quite agree with all the principles involved in the statute, but we must also be practical when it comes to methods and procedures.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, as I said before, that a summons should not be delivered in all minor cases, but I think-and I do not quite agree with the mover of this bill-that bail should be required even where the offence is punishable by death or life imprisonment.
There have been cases, in my personal experience, where people were charged with a crime punishable by death or life imprisonment who obtained bail, and rightly so. Such a bail has been granted on very rare occasions and only after due reflection and serious consideration of the record of the accused and of the offence. I do not see why this type of crime should be automatically excluded. Mr. Speaker, there is still much to be said on this question. I think that, up to now, the judges have been allowed to set the standards of bail.
From my own experience again, I may mention that I have yet to meet a lawyer who, on the morning of an appearance in court, or at any other time, could determine in advance or know how or when his client would be freed, or why he should not be.
Criticism must necessarily be avoided. The arbitrary and the abuses must particularly be avoided, and only through a much greater consideration of this question and, I must admit, not only through a suggestion that everybody be freed in the future, except in rare cases, can this problem be solved.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) suggested that this bill should be submitted for consideration to the standing committee of the house. I fully agree with him. Not only that, but I am convinced that it should be submitted to the committee on justice and legal affairs. This matter has been under consideration for too long and it is too vital to the freedom of individuals to let such anachronisms subsist.
The Leader of the Opposition was right in saying that we should be ashamed for not having legislated on this matter long ago. I hope that we will have the opportunity to 27053-1051

consider a government bill amending the Criminal Code in that respect.
More than that, we should not wait until a revision or a complete reform of the Criminal Code is made to solve that problem, because it is urgent. If, after studying that problem in committee, we can get directives, I feel that the government will have to propose amendments. If need be, the government should introduce a bill even before the committee has submitted its report. I am convinced, besides, that the government has in the Department of Justice a bill already prepared about that. It is a matter of time and of knowing when such a bill should be introduced in the house.
I think that the leaders of the various parties should come to an agreement so that a bill in that respect can be introduced by the government and even discussed by the committee of the whole House of Commons.
It is too important a matter. The Bill of Rights is flouted every day in our courts of justice, as concerns the release on bail of the accused.
And I would certainly be one of the first to approve any legislation by the government which could improve that matter of bail in our courts of justice.
